claims.text: Dynamic mechanical loading causes local grain-boundary amorphization in CoCrFeMnNi.
Grain-boundary amorphization forms an ultra-nanocrystalline, near-surface amorphous layer.
The dynamically formed layer reduces friction at grain boundaries.
Reduced grain-boundary friction facilitates stress redistribution.
Stress redistribution delays failure.
The amorphous layer produces an inverse Hall–Petch effect.
The proposed inverse Hall–Petch effect enhances ductility while maintaining high strength.
The initial bulk CoCrFeMnNi alloy has a stable coarse-grained microstructure with well-defined grain boundaries.
Incremental strain-rate testing can reveal the evolution of grain size and the formation of an amorphous surface layer when combined with rapid ex-situ and in-situ characterization.
An inert atmosphere or ultra-high vacuum prevents oxidation sufficiently to isolate intrinsic deformation processes.
Dynamic loading induces amorphization through local shear at grain boundaries.
The amorphous layer reduces barriers to dislocation movement.
Samples that form the amorphous layer will have lower friction coefficients than the coarse-grained baseline without dynamic amorphization.
Samples that form the amorphous layer will have greater ductility than the baseline.
Samples that form the amorphous layer will maintain high strength relative to the baseline.
Formation of the amorphous layer will improve work hardening during dynamic loading.
The proposed behavior is limited to dynamically loaded bulk CoCrFeMnNi in inert environments or ultra-high vacuum.
Oxidizing conditions or static loading may suppress or alter the amorphization process.
Dislocation motion or twinning may also contribute to the observed mechanical response.
Failure to detect the amorphous layer, or failure to correlate it with lower friction and enhanced ductility, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The same proposed layer is described as both ultra-nanocrystalline and amorphous without specifying a nanocrystal–amorphous composite or distinct regions; a fully amorphous phase is not itself crystalline.
